stimuli.title: Pollinating date palms
stimuli.text: Date palms grow as separate male and female trees, and only the female trees bear fruit. In the wild, wind and insects carry pollen from one to the other, but the results are uneven: many flowers are never pollinated, and the harvest suffers. For this reason, growers in oases have long done the work themselves. When the flowers open in spring, a worker climbs each female tree and ties a few strands of male flowers among its blossoms. One male tree can supply enough pollen for dozens of female trees, so a well-run grove needs only a handful of them. This saves space for the trees that matter most to the farmer. The method is slow and tiring, and some modern farms now blow pollen onto the trees with machines. Even so, many growers still prefer the old way, which they trust to set more fruit.

stimuli.title: How paper travelled west
stimuli.text: Paper was first made in China, where workers soaked plant fibres, beat them into a pulp and dried thin sheets on screens. For centuries the method stayed in the east. In the eighth century it reached Samarkand, a trading city in Central Asia, and from there it spread quickly through the Islamic world. Baghdad soon had paper mills of its own. Officials there welcomed the new material because it was cheaper than parchment, which was made from animal skin, and harder to alter without leaving a mark. That made it well suited to government records. As paper became common, books grew less costly, and libraries and booksellers multiplied in the cities of the region. Centuries later, papermaking crossed into Europe, where it would one day meet the printing press.

stimuli.title: Fresh water from the sea
stimuli.text: Many coastal countries with little rainfall turn seawater into drinking water. The older method is thermal: seawater is heated until it boils, and the steam, which leaves the salt behind, is cooled back into water. It works well but burns a great deal of fuel. Most new plants instead use reverse osmosis, pushing seawater at high pressure through membranes with pores so small that salt cannot pass. This takes far less energy, although the membranes must be cleaned and replaced regularly. Both methods leave behind brine, a very salty liquid that is usually returned to the sea. If it is released in one place, it can harm the plants and animals on the seabed nearby, so engineers spread it through long pipes with many outlets. Cutting this damage is now as important to designers as cutting cost.

stimuli.title: Sleep and memory
stimuli.text: For a long time, sleep was thought of as a pause in the brain's work. Research over the past few decades suggests otherwise. In many experiments, people who learned a list of words or a new skill and then slept recalled it better the next day than people who stayed awake for the same number of hours. Scientists believe that during sleep the brain replays some of the day's experiences, strengthening the connections that hold new memories. Not every stage of sleep seems to do the same job, which is one reason a full night appears to matter more than a short nap. None of this means that students can learn while asleep. It does suggest that a night of rest after studying is part of learning, not time taken away from it.

stimuli.title: The camel's hump
stimuli.text: A common belief holds that a camel stores water in its hump. In fact, the hump is mostly fat. Keeping fat in one place, rather than spread under the skin, may help the animal lose heat from the rest of its body. The camel's real defences against thirst lie elsewhere. It can lose a large share of its body water and keep working, a loss that would kill most mammals. Its kidneys produce very concentrated urine, and its body temperature is allowed to rise during the day, which reduces sweating. When water is finally found, a camel can drink an enormous amount in minutes and recover quickly.

stimuli.title: The honeybee's dance
stimuli.text: When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a dance on the honeycomb. In the waggle dance, she runs a short straight line while shaking her body, then circles back and repeats it. The angle of the straight run tells the other bees the direction of the food compared with the position of the sun. The length of the waggle tells them how far away it is. Bees that follow the dance then fly out and search the area it describes. Remarkably, this message is given in the dark interior of the hive, so the followers learn it by touch and vibration rather than by sight.

stimuli.title: Corals of the Red Sea
stimuli.text: Around the world, coral reefs are suffering as the oceans warm. When the water stays too hot for too long, corals expel the tiny algae that live inside them and give them food and colour. The coral turns white, an event known as bleaching, and may die if the heat lasts. Some reefs in the northern Red Sea, however, have so far coped with warm water better than many others. One explanation is that their ancestors reached the area through waters at the sea's southern end that are much hotter, so only heat-tolerant corals survived the journey. Scientists study these reefs in the hope of learning how other corals might be helped.

stimuli.title: The Hejaz Railway
stimuli.text: At the start of the twentieth century, the journey from Damascus to Medina took pilgrims many weeks by camel caravan. The Hejaz Railway was built to shorten it. Work began in 1900, and the line reached Medina in 1908, cutting the trip to a few days. Building it was hard: water had to be carried to work camps in the desert, and floods sometimes washed away the track laid across dry riverbeds. The planners hoped to extend the line to Mecca, but that section was never built. During the First World War the railway carried troops and supplies, and raiders repeatedly blew up its bridges and track. After the war, much of the southern part was abandoned. Some of its stone stations still stand today, reminders of an ambitious project that served its full route for only about ten years.

stimuli.title: Mangroves
stimuli.text: Mangroves are trees that grow where few others can: in the salty, muddy water of sheltered coasts. Some kinds keep salt out at their roots, while others take it in and get rid of it through their leaves. Their tangled roots slow the waves and trap mud, so a belt of mangroves can protect a shoreline from erosion and storms. The calm water among the roots also shelters young fish and shrimp, many of which later move out to reefs and the open sea. For these reasons, the loss of mangroves can harm fishing far from the coast where they grew. In many countries, including several around the Red Sea and the Gulf, people are now planting mangrove seedlings to restore forests that were cleared.

stimuli.title: Numbers that changed arithmetic
stimuli.text: The digits used in most of the world today began in India, where a system of ten symbols, including a sign for zero, let any number be written by place value. In the ninth century, the scholar al-Khwarizmi, working in Baghdad, wrote a book explaining how to calculate with these Indian numerals, and the method spread across the Islamic world. Europeans learned of it later, partly through Latin translations of his work. Even then, the change was slow. Many merchants and officials preferred Roman numerals, which they knew well, and some feared that the new digits could be altered easily on accounts. In time, the ease of written calculation won them over. Today the symbols are often called Arabic numerals, a name that recalls the route by which they reached Europe rather than the place where they began.

stimuli.title: Moving dunes
stimuli.text: A sand dune may look fixed, but many dunes travel. Wind blowing steadily from one direction pushes grains up the gentle slope on the windward side. At the top, the sand piles up until it becomes unstable and slides down the steep slope on the other side, called the slip face. Grain by grain, the whole dune creeps forward. Small dunes move faster than large ones, because the wind needs to shift less sand to advance them. In some deserts a dune can cover several metres in a year, burying roads and fences in its path. To slow them, people plant hardy shrubs or put up fences that make the wind drop its load of sand before it reaches what they want to protect.

stimuli.title: Falconry
stimuli.text: Falconry, the art of hunting with trained birds of prey, has been practised in Arabia for many centuries. A falconer earns the bird's trust slowly, feeding it by hand and getting it used to his voice. A leather hood placed over the bird's head keeps it calm, since it cannot see what might alarm it. Once trained, the falcon is released to chase its quarry and returns to the falconer's glove. In the past, falcons helped families add meat to their diet in the desert; today the sport is valued mainly as a living tradition. In 2010 UNESCO added falconry to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity, recognising it as a practice shared by many countries.

stimuli.title: The octopus in disguise
stimuli.text: Few animals hide as well as the octopus. Its skin holds thousands of small sacs of colour, each opened or closed by tiny muscles, so it can change colour in a fraction of a second. It can also raise bumps on its skin to copy the texture of rock or coral. Strangely, most octopuses are thought to be colour-blind. How they match their surroundings so closely is still debated: one idea is that their skin itself may sense light. Whatever the answer, the disguise is a matter of survival, because the octopus has no shell to protect its soft body.

stimuli.title: Solar panels in the desert
stimuli.text: Deserts seem ideal places for solar power: the sun shines on most days, and there is plenty of open land. Yet the desert also works against the panels. Dust settles on their surfaces and blocks sunlight, and a thick layer can cut a panel's output sharply within weeks. Washing panels with water is costly where water is scarce, so some plants use robots that sweep them dry each night. Heat is a second problem. Solar cells turn sunlight into electricity less efficiently as they get hotter, so a panel produces less power on a scorching afternoon than its sunshine alone would suggest.

questions.explanation: 15% of 240 is $0.15 \times 240 = 36$. A quick check: 10% is 24 and 5% is 12, and $24 + 12 = 36$.

questions.stem: A car travels 180 km in 2 hours and 15 minutes. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: 2 hours 15 minutes is 2.25 hours, so the speed is $180 \div 2.25 = 80$ km/h. Dividing by 2.5 or by 3 treats the 15 minutes as half an hour or a whole one.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{2}{3} + \frac{3}{4}$?
questions.explanation: Use the common denominator 12: $\frac{8}{12} + \frac{9}{12} = \frac{17}{12}$. Adding tops and bottoms separately gives $\frac{5}{7}$, which is wrong.

questions.stem: The ratio of boys to girls in a class is 3 : 5. If there are 40 students, how many are girls?
questions.explanation: The class has $3 + 5 = 8$ parts, so each part is $40 \div 8 = 5$ students. Girls are 5 parts: $5 \times 5 = 25$. 15 is the number of boys.

questions.stem: What is the next number in the sequence 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ...?
questions.explanation: The differences are 4, 6, 8 and 10, growing by 2 each time, so the next difference is 12 and $30 + 12 = 42$.

questions.stem: What is the value of $3^4 - 2^5$?
questions.explanation: $3^4 = 81$ and $2^5 = 32$, so $81 - 32 = 49$. Multiplying instead of raising to a power gives $12 - 10 = 2$, and swapping bases and exponents gives $64 - 65 = -1$.

questions.stem: A shirt costs SAR 120 after a 20% discount. What was its original price?
questions.explanation: The sale price is 80% of the original, so the original is $120 \div 0.8 = 150$. Adding 20% to 120 gives 144, which takes 20% of the wrong amount.

questions.stem: Five workers build a wall in 12 days. Working at the same rate, how many days would 6 workers take?
questions.explanation: The job takes $5 \times 12 = 60$ worker-days, so 6 workers need $60 \div 6 = 10$ days. More workers finish sooner, so the answer must be under 12.

questions.stem: What is the average of 14, 18, 23 and 25?
A bag holds 4 red, 6 blue and 10 green balls. One ball is picked at random. What is the probability that it is blue?
questions.explanation: There are $4 + 6 + 10 = 20$ balls and 6 are blue, so the probability is $\frac{6}{20} = \frac{3}{10}$. Comparing blue only with the other 14 balls gives $\frac{3}{7}$.

questions.stem: On a map with a scale of 1 : 50,000, two towns are 6 cm apart. How far apart are they in reality?
questions.explanation: 6 cm on the map is $6 \times 50{,}000 = 300{,}000$ cm. There are 100,000 cm in a kilometre, so the distance is 3 km.

questions.stem:
**First value:** $\frac{3}{7}$

**Second value:** $0.43$

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: $\frac{3}{7}$ is about 0.4286, which is less than 0.43. So the second value is greater.

questions.stem:
$n$ is a positive whole number.

**First value:** $n^2$

**Second value:** $2n$

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: For $n = 1$, $n^2 = 1$ is less than $2n = 2$. For $n = 2$ they are equal, and for $n = 3$, $9$ is more than $6$. The relationship changes with $n$.

questions.stem:
**First value:** 20% of 50

**Second value:** 50% of 20

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: 20% of 50 is 10 and 50% of 20 is 10. Swapping the percent and the number gives the same product.

questions.stem: A rectangle is 12 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is the length of its diagonal?
questions.explanation: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 12 and 5: $\sqrt{144 + 25} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ cm. 7 is just $12 - 5$, and the diagonal must be longer than the longer side.

questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure 48° and 67°. What is the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°, so the third is $180 - 48 - 67 = 65°$. 115° is the sum of the two given angles.

questions.stem: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. Using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$, what is its circumference?
questions.explanation: Circumference is $2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 44$ cm. 154 is the area, $\pi r^2$.

questions.stem: What is the area of a triangle with a base of 10 cm and a height of 6 cm?
questions.explanation: Area is half the base times the height: $\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 6 = 30$ cm². 60 forgets the half.

questions.stem:
A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. A square has sides of 9 cm.

**First value:** Area of the circle in cm²

**Second value:** Area of the square in cm²

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: The circle's radius is 5, so its area is $25\pi$, about 78.5 cm². The square's area is $9^2 = 81$ cm², which is greater.

questions.stem:
In triangle ABC, angle A is 50° and angle B is 60°.

**First value:** Angle C

**Second value:** Angle A + 20°

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: Angle C is $180 - 50 - 60 = 70°$, and angle A + 20° is also 70°.

questions.stem: If $3x - 7 = 11$, what is $x$?
questions.explanation: Add 7 to both sides: $3x = 18$. Divide by 3: $x = 6$. Subtracting 7 instead of adding gives $3x = 4$.

questions.stem: Which expression equals $(x + 3)^2 - (x - 3)^2$?
questions.explanation: $(x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 6x + 9$ and $(x - 3)^2 = x^2 - 6x + 9$. Subtracting leaves $12x$. Adding them instead gives $2x^2 + 18$.

questions.stem:
$a + b = 10$ and $a - b = 4$.

**First value:** $a$

**Second value:** $2b$

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: Adding the equations gives $2a = 14$, so $a = 7$ and $b = 3$. Then $2b = 6$, which is less than 7.

questions.stem: How many books did the library lend in the four months altogether?
questions.explanation: $120 + 150 + 90 + 140 = 500$. Each of the other totals counts one month twice.

questions.stem: By what percent did loans rise from January to February?
questions.explanation: The rise is $150 - 120 = 30$ books. As a share of January's 120, that is $\frac{30}{120} = 25\%$. Dividing by February's 150 gives 20%, which uses the wrong base.

questions.stem: How much does the family spend on food each month?
How much more does the family spend on rent than it saves each month?
questions.explanation: Rent is 35% and savings 10%, a difference of 25%. 25% of SAR 8,000 is SAR 2,000. Rent alone is SAR 2,800.

questions.stem: How many minutes are there in 2.4 hours?
questions.explanation: $2.4 \times 60 = 144$ minutes. Reading 2.4 hours as 2 hours 40 minutes gives 160, and as 2 hours 4 minutes gives 124.

questions.stem: Ahmed saves SAR 350 a month. How many months will it take him to save SAR 4,900?
The price of a book rose from SAR 40 to SAR 50. By what percent did it rise?
questions.explanation: The rise is SAR 10 on an original price of SAR 40, and $\frac{10}{40} = 25\%$. Dividing by the new price, 50, gives 20%.

questions.stem: What is the least common multiple of 6, 8 and 12?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36 and so on. 24 is the first one that 8 also divides, and 6 divides it too.

questions.stem: If 3 kg of dates cost SAR 45, how much do 5 kg cost at the same price?
questions.explanation: One kilogram costs $45 \div 3 = 15$, so 5 kg cost $5 \times 15 = 75$.

questions.stem: A train leaves at 9:45 and arrives at 13:20 the same day. How long is the journey?
questions.explanation: From 9:45 to 13:45 is 4 hours, or 240 minutes. The train arrives 25 minutes before 13:45, so the trip takes $240 - 25 = 215$ minutes.

questions.stem: What is $0.25 \times 0.4$?
questions.explanation: $25 \times 4 = 100$, and the two factors have three decimal places between them, so the product is 0.100, which is 0.1. Adding them gives 0.65.

questions.stem: The mean of five numbers is 12. Four of them are 10, 11, 13 and 15. What is the fifth number?
questions.explanation: Five numbers with a mean of 12 add up to 60. The four known numbers add up to 49, so the fifth is $60 - 49 = 11$.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{3}{4}$ of $\frac{2}{5}$ of 200?
questions.explanation: $\frac{2}{5}$ of 200 is 80, and $\frac{3}{4}$ of 80 is 60. 80 stops after the first step, and 150 takes only $\frac{3}{4}$ of 200.

questions.stem: A tank holds 600 litres and is 40% full. How many more litres are needed to fill it?
questions.explanation: It holds $0.4 \times 600 = 240$ litres now, so it needs $600 - 240 = 360$ more. 240 is the amount already in the tank.

questions.stem: Which number is a factor of 84 but not of 63?
questions.explanation: $84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$ and $63 = 3^2 \times 7$. 3, 7 and 21 divide both numbers; 4 divides 84 but not 63.

questions.stem:
**First value:** $(-3)^2$

**Second value:** $-3^2$

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: $(-3)^2 = 9$ because the bracket squares the negative number. In $-3^2$ only the 3 is squared, so it is $-9$.

questions.stem:
A runner covers 1.2 km in 6 minutes at a steady pace.

**First value:** Distance covered in 15 minutes, in km

**Second value:** 3

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: The runner covers $1.2 \div 6 = 0.2$ km a minute, so 15 minutes gives $0.2 \times 15 = 3$ km.

questions.stem:
**First value:** $\sqrt{80}$

**Second value:** 9

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: $9 = \sqrt{81}$, and $\sqrt{80}$ is less than $\sqrt{81}$, so the second value is greater.

questions.stem: A cube has a volume of 64 cm³. What is the total area of its six faces?
questions.explanation: The side is $\sqrt[3]{64} = 4$ cm, each face is $4^2 = 16$ cm², and six faces give 96 cm². 16 cm² is a single face.

questions.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon?
questions.explanation: A polygon with $n$ sides has interior angles adding up to $(n - 2) \times 180°$. For six sides that is $4 \times 180 = 720°$. 540° is the pentagon's total.

questions.stem: A square has a perimeter of 36 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Each side is $36 \div 4 = 9$ cm, so the area is $9^2 = 81$ cm². Squaring the perimeter gives 324.

questions.stem: Point A is at (1, 2) and point B is at (7, 10). What is the distance between them?
questions.explanation: The points are 6 apart across and 8 apart up, so the distance is $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$. Adding 6 and 8 gives 14.

questions.stem: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides of 4 cm and 10 cm. The smaller triangle's height is 6 cm. What is the larger triangle's height?
questions.explanation: The scale factor is $10 \div 4 = 2.5$, so the height is $6 \times 2.5 = 15$ cm. Adding the difference in sides, 6, gives 12, but similar shapes scale by multiplying.

questions.stem:
A rectangle has an area of 36 cm².

**First value:** Its perimeter in cm

**Second value:** 24

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: A 6 by 6 square has a perimeter of 24, equal to the second value, but a 4 by 9 rectangle has a perimeter of 26. The first value can be equal or greater.

questions.stem: Which values of $x$ satisfy $2x + 5 < 17$?
questions.explanation: Subtract 5: $2x < 12$. Divide by 2: $x < 6$. Dividing by a positive number keeps the direction of the sign.

questions.stem:
$x$ is a real number.

**First value:** $x^2 + 1$

**Second value:** $2x$

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: $x^2 + 1 - 2x = (x - 1)^2$, which is 0 when $x = 1$ and positive otherwise. The values are equal at $x = 1$ and the first is greater everywhere else, so no single answer holds.

questions.stem: What is the mean number of visitors over the five days?
questions.explanation: The total is $240 + 180 + 210 + 150 + 300 = 1{,}080$, and $1{,}080 \div 5 = 216$. Dividing by 4 instead of 5 gives 270.

questions.stem: What is the median number of visitors?
questions.explanation: In order the values are 150, 180, 210, 240 and 300, so the middle one is 210.

questions.stem: On which day were there 25% more visitors than on Sunday?
questions.explanation: 25% more than 240 is $240 \times 1.25 = 300$, the Thursday figure.

questions.stem: How many students in the club play neither sport?
questions.explanation: Football or basketball or both: $22 + 18 - 5 = 35$ students, since the 5 who play both are counted twice. That leaves $45 - 35 = 10$.

questions.stem: How many students play football only?
questions.explanation: Of the 22 football players, 5 also play basketball, so $22 - 5 = 17$ play football only.

questions.stem:
**SURGEON : SCALPEL**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: A surgeon works with a scalpel, as a painter works with a brush. A hospital and a stage are places, not tools.

questions.stem:
**DROP : OCEAN**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: A drop is one tiny unit of the vast ocean, as a grain of sand is one tiny unit of a desert. Rain falls from a cloud, which is a different relationship.

questions.stem:
**GLOVE : HAND**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: A glove is worn to cover the hand, as a sock covers the foot. A scarf may be made of wool, which is a material, not a body part it covers.

questions.stem:
**FRAGILE : BREAK**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: Something fragile breaks easily, as something flammable burns easily. A solid can melt, but being solid does not make it melt easily.

questions.stem:
**SPARK : BLAZE**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: A spark is a tiny fire and a blaze a huge one, as a trickle is a tiny flow and a flood a huge one. An ember leaves ash, which is what remains after burning.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the other three?
questions.explanation: The violin, guitar and harp are string instruments. The trumpet is a brass instrument played by blowing.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the other three?
questions.explanation: The kilogram, gram and tonne measure mass. The litre measures volume.

questions.stem:
The lecture was so ____ that half the audience fell asleep before the end.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: People fall asleep in a dull lecture, so "tedious" fits. A gripping lecture would keep them awake.

questions.stem:
Unlike his brother, who spends money freely, Khalid is ____ and saves most of his salary.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: "Unlike" contrasts Khalid with a free spender, and saving most of his salary makes him thrifty. Being wealthy does not explain the saving.

questions.stem:
The evidence was ____: it could be read as supporting either side of the argument.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Evidence that supports either side is open to more than one reading, which is what ambiguous means. Decisive evidence would settle the argument.

questions.stem:
The __thick__ fog __improved__ visibility so much that the airport __cancelled__ all morning __flights__.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: Thick fog lowers visibility, and that is why flights are cancelled. "Improved" should be "reduced".

questions.stem:
Since the restaurant was __empty__, we __waited__ an hour for a __table__ __near__ the window.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: Waiting an hour for a table means the restaurant was crowded. In an empty restaurant every table is free.

questions.stem:
Many desert animals are __active__ at night, __avoiding__ the __cool__ hours of the midday __sun__.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: The midday sun brings the hottest hours of the desert day, which the animals avoid. "Cool" should be "hot".

questions.stem:
Working __slowly__ because they were racing against time, the __rescue__ team __freed__ the trapped miners by __dawn__.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: A team racing against time works fast, not slowly.

questions.stem: Why was the Hejaz Railway built, according to the passage?
options: To carry troops in the war
To bring water to desert camps
To shorten the journey to Medina
questions.explanation: The passage says the railway was built to shorten a journey that took many weeks by caravan. It carried troops later, and the Mecca section was never built.

questions.stem: Which difficulty in building the line does the passage mention?
options: A shortage of stone for stations
questions.explanation: The passage says floods sometimes washed away the track laid across dry riverbeds. Raids happened during the war, after the line was built.

questions.stem: In the passage, "that section" refers to the line:
questions.explanation: The sentence says the planners hoped to extend the line to Mecca, "but that section was never built": the part beyond Medina to Mecca.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about the railway's working life?
options: It was abandoned before the war
It is still used by most pilgrims
Its whole route was in use only briefly
It never reached Medina at all
questions.explanation: The line reached Medina in 1908 and much of the southern part was abandoned after the First World War, so the full route served for only about ten years, as the last sentence says.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Where mangroves grow and how fishing harms them
How mangroves take in salt and why it harms them
Why mangroves are cleared and how to stop it
Why mangroves matter and are being replanted
questions.explanation: The passage explains how mangroves survive salt water, how they protect coasts and young fish, and why people are restoring them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how do some mangroves deal with salt?
options: They remove it through their leaves
They pass it to nearby fish
They store it in their trunks
They grow only in fresh water
questions.explanation: The passage says some kinds keep salt out at their roots, while others take it in and get rid of it through their leaves.

questions.stem: Why can the loss of mangroves harm fishing far from the coast?
options: Their mud flows out and covers the reefs
Many sea fish start life among their roots
Fishing boats shelter among the trees
Their leaves are food for deep-sea fish
questions.explanation: Young fish and shrimp shelter among mangrove roots and later move out to reefs and the open sea, so fewer mangroves means fewer fish elsewhere.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "restore" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: People plant seedlings to "restore forests that were cleared": to bring back forests that had been lost. Protecting would apply to forests still standing.

questions.stem:
**LIBRARY : BOOKS**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: A library is a place where books are collected and kept, as an archive is where records are kept. An author writes pages but is not a place.

questions.stem:
**EXHAUSTED : TIRED**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: Exhausted is an extreme form of tired, as furious is an extreme form of annoyed. "Quiet : silent" puts the milder word first, the reverse order.

questions.stem:
**CARPENTER : WOOD**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: A carpenter works with wood as the material, as a tailor works with cloth. An oven is a baker's tool, and a wall is what a mason builds.

questions.stem:
**ARID : RAIN**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: An arid place lacks rain, as a silent place lacks sound. Something wet has water, the opposite relationship.

questions.stem:
**ACCELERATE : SPEED**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: To accelerate is to increase speed, as to amplify is to increase volume. To lower is to decrease height, the opposite direction.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the other three?
questions.explanation: The sparrow, falcon and pigeon are birds. The bat flies too, but it is a mammal.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the other three?
questions.explanation: Generous, kind and charitable describe giving freely. Stingy means unwilling to give or spend.

questions.stem:
Once a ____ fishing village, the town has ____ into a busy port with thousands of residents.

Which words best complete the sentence?
questions.explanation: "Once" contrasts the past with the present busy port, so the village was quiet and the town has grown. "Declined" cannot lead to a busy port.

questions.stem:
Because the instructions were ____, every student completed the experiment without asking for help.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: No one needed help because the instructions were clear and fully stated, which is what explicit means. Confusing instructions would lead to questions.

questions.stem:
The athlete's recovery was ____; within a week of the injury she was training again.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Training again within a week shows a fast recovery. A gradual recovery would take much longer.

questions.stem:
An __expert__ in her field, she __rarely__ needed to consult the __manual__, which she knew __poorly__.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: An expert who rarely needs the manual knows it well. "Poorly" clashes with both "expert" and "rarely".

questions.stem:
Since __smoking__ damages the lungs, doctors __recommend__ it to patients who want to __protect__ their __health__.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: Because smoking damages the lungs, doctors warn patients who want to protect their health against it. "Recommend" breaks the cause and effect.

questions.stem:
The __economical__ car uses __little__ fuel, so its owners __spend__ __more__ on petrol than other drivers.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: A car that uses little fuel costs its owners less on petrol, not more.

questions.stem:
The __loud__ music from the party __kept__ the neighbours __awake__, and they __thanked__ the hosts the next morning.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: Neighbours kept awake by loud music would complain to the hosts, not thank them.

questions.stem: Where did the digits used today begin, according to the passage?
questions.explanation: The first sentence says the digits began in India. Baghdad is where al-Khwarizmi wrote about them, and the passage says the name Arabic numerals recalls their route, not their origin.

questions.stem: Why did some Europeans at first prefer Roman numerals?
options: Their rulers had banned the new digits
They knew them and distrusted the new digits
The new digits had no sign for zero
questions.explanation: The passage says merchants and officials knew Roman numerals well, and some feared the new digits could be altered easily on accounts. It says the new digits made written sums easier.

questions.stem: In the passage, the word "them" in "won them over" refers to:
questions.explanation: The ease of written calculation won over the people who had resisted: the merchants and officials who preferred Roman numerals.

questions.stem: What point does the writer make in the last sentence?
options: The name Arabic numerals reflects their route
The name was chosen by al-Khwarizmi
The digits were invented in Arabia
Europeans invented the sign for zero
questions.explanation: The writer says the name recalls "the route by which they reached Europe rather than the place where they began", which was India.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is the slip face of a dune?
options: The sand at its very top
The ground in front of it
questions.explanation: Sand piles up at the top and slides down "the steep slope on the other side, called the slip face". The gentle slope is the windward side.

questions.stem: Why do small dunes move faster than large ones?
options: Their slip faces are much steeper
Shrubs do not grow on them
The wind must shift less sand
The wind blows harder near the ground
questions.explanation: The passage says the wind needs to shift less sand to advance a small dune.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "creeps" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: "Grain by grain, the whole dune creeps forward": it advances slowly and steadily.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how do fences help protect roads from dunes?
options: They make the wind drop sand early
They stop the wind from blowing
They push sand back up the dune
They hold the slip face in place
questions.explanation: Fences "make the wind drop its load of sand before it reaches" what people want to protect. They slow the wind, but nothing says they stop it.

questions.stem:
**EYE : SIGHT**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: The eye is the organ of sight, as the ear is the organ of hearing. An earring is worn on the ear, and a nose is part of a face, which is a part-to-whole relationship.

questions.stem:
**PREDICT : FUTURE**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: To predict is to speak about the future, as to recall is to bring back the past. One plans a meeting, but a meeting is not a time.

questions.stem:
**ISLAND : WATER**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: An island is land surrounded by water, as an oasis is a fertile place surrounded by desert. A peninsula is joined to the land on one side, so it is not surrounded.

questions.stem:
**JUDGE : VERDICT**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: A judge gives a verdict, as a referee gives a decision. A lawyer serves a client but does not hand one down.

questions.stem:
**OBSTINATE : STUBBORN**

Which pair has the same relationship?
questions.explanation: Obstinate and stubborn mean the same thing, as do diligent and hardworking. Generous and selfish are opposites.

questions.stem: Which word does not belong with the other three?
questions.explanation: Nine, fifteen and twenty-one are all odd multiples of 3. Twenty-eight is even and is not a multiple of 3.

questions.stem:
Although the critics ____ the film, audiences loved it and filled cinemas for months.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: "Although" sets the critics against the audiences who loved the film, so the critics rejected it. Praising it would leave no contrast.

questions.stem:
The new road was meant to ____ traffic, but it ____ congestion instead, as more drivers chose the main street.

Which words best complete the sentence?
questions.explanation: "Meant to ... but ... instead" signals the opposite of the plan: the road was meant to ease traffic and made congestion worse.

questions.stem:
Her reply was so ____ that no one could tell whether she had accepted the offer.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: A reply that leaves everyone unsure avoids giving a clear answer: it is evasive. A direct reply would settle the question.

questions.stem:
On the __icy__ road, the driver __increased__ his speed to stay __safe__ and __avoid__ skidding.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: On an icy road a driver slows down to stay safe. "Increased" should be "reduced".

questions.stem:
The __drought__ lasted for __years__, and the lake __expanded__ until its old pier stood on dry __ground__.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: A long drought shrinks a lake, leaving its pier on dry ground. "Expanded" is the opposite.

questions.stem:
After the bad news, the __family__ felt __delighted__, __cancelled__ their trip and stayed __home__.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: Bad news that makes a family cancel a trip upsets them. "Delighted" does not fit.

questions.stem:
The __thin__ ice on the lake carried heavy __trucks__ __safely__ all __winter__.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: Only thick ice can carry heavy trucks safely all winter. "Thin" should be "thick".

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does a falconer put a hood on the bird?
questions.explanation: The hood keeps the bird calm "since it cannot see what might alarm it".

questions.stem: How does the passage say falconry has changed?
options: Falcons are now trained without hoods
It is now practised only in Arabia
It now provides most families' meat
It is now valued mostly as a tradition
questions.explanation: In the past falcons helped families add meat to their diet; today the sport is valued mainly as a living tradition.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "quarry" most nearly means:
options: a place where stone is cut
questions.explanation: The falcon "is released to chase its quarry", so the quarry is the animal it hunts. A stone pit is another meaning of the word that does not fit here.

questions.stem: How does an octopus change colour so quickly, according to the passage?
options: Muscles open and close sacs of colour
Its blood rises to the surface
questions.explanation: The passage says its skin holds thousands of colour sacs, each opened or closed by tiny muscles. The passage also says it has no shell.

questions.stem: What does the writer find strange about the octopus?
options: It can raise bumps on its skin
It matches colours it may not see
It has no bones in its arms
questions.explanation: Right after describing the disguise, the writer says that, "strangely", most octopuses are thought to be colour-blind.

questions.stem: Why is disguise "a matter of survival" for the octopus?
options: It moves too slowly to escape
Its soft body has no shell
questions.explanation: The last sentence gives the reason: the octopus has no shell to protect its soft body.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Deserts suit solar power but also hinder it
Deserts suit solar power but lack cooling water
Robots clean panels well but cost too much
Heat helps panels but dust harms them
questions.explanation: The passage says deserts seem ideal but then describes dust and heat working against the panels. It never says panels need cooling water or that robots cost too much, and heat lowers output rather than helping.

questions.stem: Why do some desert plants clean panels with robots?
options: Washing with water is costly there
questions.explanation: The passage says washing with water is costly where water is scarce, so some plants sweep the panels dry with robots.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a panel on a scorching afternoon:
options: stops working until it has cooled down
makes more power because the sun is strongest
makes less power than its light would allow
needs washing with scarce water first
questions.explanation: Solar cells turn sunlight into electricity less efficiently as they get hotter, so the panel produces less power than its sunshine alone would suggest. Strong sun does not make up for the heat, and the panel keeps working.

questions.stem: What is 35% of 80?
questions.explanation: $0.35 \times 80 = 28$. A check: 10% of 80 is 8, so 30% is 24, and 5% adds 4 more.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides at a steady 18 km/h. How far does she ride in 40 minutes?
questions.explanation: 40 minutes is $\frac{2}{3}$ of an hour, so she rides $18 \times \frac{2}{3} = 12$ km. Multiplying 18 by 40 gives 720, which mixes hours and minutes.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{5}{6} - \frac{1}{4}$?
questions.explanation: With the common denominator 12: $\frac{10}{12} - \frac{3}{12} = \frac{7}{12}$.

questions.stem: SAR 720 is shared between Huda and Reem in the ratio 5 : 3. How much does Huda get?
questions.explanation: There are $5 + 3 = 8$ parts, each worth $720 \div 8 = 90$. Huda gets 5 parts, SAR 450; SAR 270 is Reem's share.

questions.stem: What is the next number in the sequence 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, ...?
questions.explanation: The differences are 3, 5, 7 and 9, the odd numbers in turn, so the next difference is 11 and $27 + 11 = 38$.

questions.stem: What is $2^{10} \div 2^7$?
questions.explanation: Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents: $2^{10-7} = 2^3 = 8$. 3 is the exponent, not the value.

questions.stem: A phone's price falls by 15% to SAR 1,700. What was its original price?
questions.explanation: SAR 1,700 is 85% of the original, so the original is $1{,}700 \div 0.85 = 2{,}000$. Adding 15% to 1,700 gives 1,955, which takes 15% of the wrong amount.

questions.stem: Which whole number is closest to $\sqrt{50} + \sqrt{17}$?
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{50}$ is just over 7 (since $7^2 = 49$) and $\sqrt{17}$ is just over 4 (since $4^2 = 16$), so the sum is a little over 11. Adding under the root gives $\sqrt{67}$, about 8.

questions.stem: Eight taps fill a pool in 9 hours. How long would 6 taps take at the same rate?
questions.explanation: The pool needs $8 \times 9 = 72$ tap-hours, so 6 taps take $72 \div 6 = 12$ hours. Fewer taps take longer, so the answer must be over 9.

questions.stem: The mean of four numbers is 15. When the number 21 is removed, what is the mean of the other three?
questions.explanation: The four numbers add up to $4 \times 15 = 60$. Without 21 the rest add up to 39, and $39 \div 3 = 13$.

questions.stem: What is $0.6 \div 0.03$?
questions.explanation: Multiply both numbers by 100: $60 \div 3 = 20$.

questions.stem:
**First value:** $\frac{5}{9}$

**Second value:** $\frac{4}{7}$

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: Cross-multiply: $5 \times 7 = 35$ and $4 \times 9 = 36$. Since 35 is less than 36, $\frac{5}{9}$ is less than $\frac{4}{7}$.

questions.stem:
$x$ is a number between 0 and 1.

**First value:** $x$

**Second value:** $x^2$

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: Squaring a number between 0 and 1 makes it smaller: for $x = \frac{1}{2}$, $x^2 = \frac{1}{4}$. So $x$ is always greater.

questions.stem:
A price is raised by 10%, and the new price is then cut by 10%.

**First value:** The final price

**Second value:** The original price

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: On a price of 100, the rise gives 110 and the 10% cut takes off 11, leaving 99. The cut is taken from a larger amount, so the final price is lower.

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs of 9 cm and 12 cm. How long is its hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ cm. 21 is just the two legs added.

questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°. What is each of its base angles?
questions.explanation: The two base angles are equal and share $180 - 40 = 140°$, so each is 70°.

questions.stem: A circle has a circumference of $10\pi$ cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: $2\pi r = 10\pi$ gives $r = 5$, so the area is $\pi r^2 = 25\pi$ cm². Using 10 as the radius gives $100\pi$.

questions.stem: A box is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume is length times width times height: $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$ cm³. 12 is the sum of the three edges.

questions.stem:
A square has a diagonal of 8 cm.

**First value:** The square's area in cm²

**Second value:** 32

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: A square's area is half its diagonal squared: $\frac{8^2}{2} = 32$ cm². Or: the side is $\frac{8}{\sqrt{2}}$, and its square is $\frac{64}{2} = 32$.

questions.stem:
Triangle PQR has sides of 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm.

**First value:** The angle opposite the 13 cm side

**Second value:** 85°

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: $5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13^2$, so the triangle is right-angled and the angle opposite the 13 cm side is 90°, greater than 85°.

questions.stem: If $\frac{x}{4} + 3 = 8$, what is $x$?
questions.explanation: Subtract 3: $\frac{x}{4} = 5$. Multiply by 4: $x = 20$. Dividing 5 by 4 instead gives 1.25.

questions.stem: Which expression is equal to $x^2 - 9$?
questions.explanation: $x^2 - 9$ is a difference of two squares, $x^2 - 3^2 = (x - 3)(x + 3)$. $(x - 3)^2$ expands to $x^2 - 6x + 9$.

questions.stem:
$2x + y = 11$ and $x = 3$.

**First value:** $y$

**Second value:** $x + 2$

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: With $x = 3$, $6 + y = 11$, so $y = 5$. And $x + 2 = 5$ as well.

questions.stem: In which year did the dealer sell fewer cars than the year before?
questions.explanation: Sales went from 500 in 2022 to 480 in 2023, the only fall. Every other year rose.

questions.stem: By what percent did sales rise from 2023 to 2024?
questions.explanation: The rise is $540 - 480 = 60$ cars, and $\frac{60}{480} = 12.5\%$. Dividing by 540 instead gives about 11.1%.

questions.stem: How many students chose science?
questions.explanation: Science is 25% of 600 students: $0.25 \times 600 = 150$.

questions.stem: What is the angle of the mathematics sector in the pie chart?
questions.explanation: A whole pie chart is 360°, and mathematics is 30% of it: $0.3 \times 360 = 108°$.

questions.stem: A box holds 3 white and 5 black marbles. Two are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are white?
questions.explanation: The first is white with probability $\frac{3}{8}$; then 2 of the remaining 7 are white, so $\frac{3}{8} \times \frac{2}{7} = \frac{6}{56} = \frac{3}{28}$. $\frac{9}{64}$ would be right only if the first marble were put back.

questions.stem: A recipe uses 250 g of flour for 4 people. How much flour is needed for 10 people?
questions.explanation: Each person needs $250 \div 4 = 62.5$ g, so 10 people need 625 g. 2,500 g multiplies 250 by 10 without dividing by 4 first.

questions.stem: How many seconds are there in 3 hours?
questions.explanation: One hour is $60 \times 60 = 3{,}600$ seconds, so 3 hours is $3 \times 3{,}600 = 10{,}800$ seconds. 21,600 would be 6 hours.

questions.stem: Nora read 45 pages on Monday, which was 30% of her book. How many pages does the book have?
questions.explanation: If 30% is 45 pages, 10% is 15 pages and the whole book is $15 \times 10 = 150$ pages. 135 is 45 times 3, which forgets the last 10%.

questions.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 60?
questions.explanation: $36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$ and $60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5$. They share $2^2 \times 3 = 12$. 180 is the least common multiple.

questions.stem: A car uses 8 litres of fuel for every 100 km. How much fuel does it need for 350 km?
questions.explanation: 350 km is 3.5 times 100 km, so it needs $8 \times 3.5 = 28$ litres. 43.75 comes from dividing 350 by 8.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is a multiple of both 4 and 6 but not of 8?
questions.explanation: Multiples of both 4 and 6 are multiples of 12: 24, 36 and 48 here. 24 and 48 are also multiples of 8, so 36 is the answer. 18 is not a multiple of 4.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{1}{2} \div \frac{1}{8}$?
questions.explanation: Dividing by $\frac{1}{8}$ is the same as multiplying by 8: $\frac{1}{2} \times 8 = 4$. Multiplying the fractions instead gives $\frac{1}{16}$.

questions.stem: A lesson starts at 08:50 and lasts 1 hour and 35 minutes. When does it end?
questions.explanation: One hour after 08:50 is 09:50, and 35 more minutes is 10:25.

questions.stem: What percent of 6 is 1.5?
questions.explanation: $\frac{1.5}{6} = 0.25 = 25\%$. Dividing 6 by 1.5 gives 4, or 400%, which is the wrong way round.

questions.stem: Three numbers have a median of 10 and a mean of 12. The smallest is 6. What is the largest?
questions.explanation: Three numbers with a mean of 12 add up to 36. The middle one is 10 and the smallest 6, so the largest is $36 - 10 - 6 = 20$. Subtracting only the median gives 26.

questions.stem:
**First value:** The number of days in 7 weeks

**Second value:** The number of months in 4 years

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: 7 weeks have $7 \times 7 = 49$ days and 4 years have $4 \times 12 = 48$ months.

questions.stem:
$m$ is a whole number and $5 < m < 9$.

**First value:** $m$

**Second value:** 7

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: $m$ can be 6, 7 or 8, so it can be less than, equal to or greater than 7.

**Second value:** The mean of 3 and 7

Compare the two values:
Each interior angle of a regular pentagon measures:
questions.explanation: The interior angles of a pentagon add up to $(5 - 2) \times 180 = 540°$, so each of the five equal angles is $540 \div 5 = 108°$. 72° is each exterior angle.

questions.stem: A rectangle's length is twice its width, and its perimeter is 48 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: If the width is $w$, the perimeter is $2(w + 2w) = 6w = 48$, so $w = 8$ and the length is 16. The area is $8 \times 16 = 128$ cm². 144 is the area of a square with the same perimeter.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line through the points (2, 3) and (6, 11)?
questions.explanation: Slope is the change in $y$ over the change in $x$: $\frac{11 - 3}{6 - 2} = \frac{8}{4} = 2$. Inverting it gives $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.stem: A 10 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 6 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
questions.explanation: The ladder is the hypotenuse: $\sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ m. 4 m is just $10 - 6$.

questions.stem: A semicircle has a diameter of 14 cm. Using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$, what is its area?
questions.explanation: The radius is 7 cm, so the full circle's area is $\frac{22}{7} \times 49 = 154$ cm², and half of it is 77 cm².

questions.stem:
Two angles of a triangle are each greater than 50°.

**First value:** The third angle

**Second value:** 80°

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: The two angles add up to more than 100°, so the third angle is less than $180 - 100 = 80°$.

questions.stem: If $4 - 3x \ge 13$, which of these must be true?
questions.explanation: Subtract 4: $-3x \ge 9$. Dividing by $-3$ reverses the sign: $x \le -3$.

questions.stem:
$p$ and $q$ are positive numbers and $p > q$.

**First value:** $\frac{p}{q}$

**Second value:** $\frac{q}{p}$

Compare the two values:
questions.explanation: With $p > q > 0$, $\frac{p}{q}$ is greater than 1 and $\frac{q}{p}$ is less than 1.

questions.stem: Between which two readings did the temperature rise the most?
questions.explanation: The rises are 6° from 06:00 to 09:00, 9° from 09:00 to 12:00 and 3° from 12:00 to 15:00. From 15:00 to 18:00 the temperature fell.

questions.stem: What is the range of the six temperatures?
questions.explanation: Range is the highest value minus the lowest: $36 - 18 = 18$°C.

questions.stem: What is the mean of the six temperatures?
questions.explanation: The sum is $18 + 24 + 33 + 36 + 29 + 22 = 162$, and $162 \div 6 = 27$°C. Dividing by 5 instead of 6 gives 32.4.

questions.stem: How many students study French only?
questions.explanation: Of the 16 French students, 4 also study German, so $16 - 4 = 12$ study French only.

questions.stem: How many students study neither language?
questions.explanation: French or German or both: $16 + 11 - 4 = 23$ students, since the 4 who study both are counted twice. That leaves $30 - 23 = 7$.

questions.stem:
The professor's explanation was so ____ that even beginners followed it easily.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Beginners following it easily shows the explanation was easy to understand, which is what accessible means here. An obscure or highly technical one would lose them.

questions.stem:
Prices rose sharply this year; ____, many families cut back on travel.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Cutting back on travel is a result of rising prices, so the link word must show cause and effect. "Nevertheless" would signal a contrast.

questions.stem:
Although she was ____ at first, Mona soon became the most talkative member of the club.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: "Although" sets up a contrast with becoming the most talkative member, so at first she was quiet and reserved. Outgoing would agree with the rest, not contrast with it.

questions.stem:
The writer's tone was ____, mocking the very officials he claimed to admire.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Mocking people while claiming to admire them is saying the opposite of what one means: a sarcastic tone. A sincere tone means what it says.

questions.stem:
The plan seemed ____ on paper, but in practice it proved ____ and was soon dropped.

Which words best complete the sentence?
questions.explanation: "But" contrasts the plan on paper with the plan in practice, and being dropped shows it failed: it looked sound and proved unworkable. "Risky ... reliable" and "costly ... effective" are contrasts too, but a reliable or effective plan would not be dropped.

questions.stem:
Many desert plants have ____ roots that spread wide and reach deep underground in search of water.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Roots that spread wide and reach deep cover a large area, which is what extensive means. Shallow roots stay near the surface, the opposite of what the sentence describes.

questions.stem:
Water __freezes__ at a __higher__ temperature when salt is __added__, which is why roads are __salted__ in winter.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: Salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes, which is why salted roads stay clear. "Higher" should be "lower".

questions.stem:
The __student__ had __memorised__ the poem so well that she __forgot__ every __line__ on stage.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: Having memorised the poem well, she would remember every line. "Forgot" reverses the result.

questions.stem:
The __silent__ crowd __cheered__ the runners __loudly__ as they __crossed__ the finish line.

Which underlined word does not fit the meaning of the sentence?
questions.explanation: A crowd cheering loudly is not silent. The word should be something like "excited".

questions.stem: What is $\sqrt{0.49}$?
questions.explanation: $0.7 \times 0.7 = 0.49$, so $\sqrt{0.49} = 0.7$. Halving 0.49 gives 0.245, which is not a square root.

questions.stem: What is 3.4762 rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The third decimal place is 6, which is 5 or more, so the second place rounds up from 7 to 8: 3.48.

questions.stem: Which of these fractions is the largest?
questions.explanation: As decimals they are 0.625, 0.6, about 0.583 and about 0.571, so $\frac{5}{8}$ is the largest.

questions.stem: A cylinder has a radius of 3 cm and a height of 10 cm. Using $\pi = 3.14$, what is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume is $\pi r^2 h = 3.14 \times 9 \times 10 = 282.6$ cm³. Using the diameter, 6, as the radius gives 1,130.4.

questions.stem: A trapezium has parallel sides of 6 cm and 10 cm and a height of 5 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area is the mean of the parallel sides times the height: $\frac{6 + 10}{2} \times 5 = 40$ cm². 80 forgets to halve the sum.

questions.stem: The exterior angle of a triangle at vertex C is 130°. Angle A is 70°. What is angle B?
questions.explanation: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, so $70 + B = 130$ and $B = 60°$. 110° is $180 - 70$, which ignores the exterior angle.

questions.stem: If $5x + 2 = 3x + 14$, what is $x$?
questions.explanation: Subtract $3x$ and 2 from both sides: $2x = 12$, so $x = 6$. 8 comes from adding the 2 instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: What is the value of $2a^2 - 3b$ when $a = 3$ and $b = -2$?
questions.explanation: $2 \times 3^2 = 18$ and $-3 \times (-2) = 6$, so the value is $18 + 6 = 24$. Squaring $2a$ instead of $a$ gives $36 + 6 = 42$.

questions.stem: Which expression equals $3(2x - 4) - 2(x - 5)$?
questions.explanation: $3(2x - 4) = 6x - 12$ and $-2(x - 5) = -2x + 10$. Together: $4x - 2$. Forgetting that $-2 \times -5$ is positive gives $4x - 22$.

questions.stem: If $x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$, which values can $x$ take?
questions.explanation: $x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3)$, which is zero when $x = 2$ or $x = 3$. The signs are both negative in the brackets because the middle term is $-5x$.

questions.stem: A number is doubled and then increased by 7, giving 31. What is the number?
questions.explanation: If the number is $n$, then $2n + 7 = 31$, so $2n = 24$ and $n = 12$. 24 is double the number.

questions.stem: Which values of $x$ satisfy $3x - 4 > 2x + 1$?
questions.explanation: Subtract $2x$: $x - 4 > 1$. Add 4: $x > 5$.

questions.stem: If $a = 2b$ and $b = 3c$, what is $a$ in terms of $c$?
questions.explanation: Substitute $b = 3c$ into $a = 2b$: $a = 2 \times 3c = 6c$. Adding the multipliers gives $5c$.

questions.stem: The sum of two consecutive whole numbers is 47. What is the larger number?
questions.explanation: If the numbers are $n$ and $n + 1$, then $2n + 1 = 47$, so $n = 23$ and the larger number is 24. 23 is the smaller one.

questions.stem: For $x \ne 0$, what is $\frac{6x^2 + 9x}{3x}$?
questions.explanation: Divide each term by $3x$: $\frac{6x^2}{3x} = 2x$ and $\frac{9x}{3x} = 3$. Dividing only the first term gives $2x + 9$.

questions.stem: If $\frac{x + 1}{3} = \frac{x - 1}{2}$, what is $x$?
questions.explanation: Cross-multiply: $2(x + 1) = 3(x - 1)$, so $2x + 2 = 3x - 3$ and $x = 5$.

questions.stem: What was the total rainfall over the five months?
What share of the five months' total rainfall fell in December?
questions.explanation: December had 36 mm of the 120 mm total, and $\frac{36}{120} = 30\%$. 36% mistakes the millimetres for a percent.

questions.stem: In which month was the rainfall half of December's?
questions.explanation: Half of December's 36 mm is 18 mm, which fell in November. March had a third of December's rain.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of students who chose football to those who chose tennis?
questions.explanation: 45 to 15 simplifies to 3 : 1 by dividing both by 15. 1 : 3 puts tennis first.

questions.stem: What is the mean number of students per sport?
questions.explanation: 100 students across 4 sports gives $100 \div 4 = 25$. 22.5 is the median of the four bars.

questions.stem: If 20 more students joined and all chose running, what percent of all the students would choose running?
questions.explanation: Running would have $10 + 20 = 30$ of $100 + 20 = 120$ students, and $\frac{30}{120} = 25\%$. 30% forgets that the total also grew.
